mn35:1.2: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Vesali in the Great Wood in the Hall with the Peaked Roof.
mn35:2.1: Now on that occasion Saccaka the Nigantha’s son was staying at Vesāli, a debater and a clever speaker, regarded by many as a saint.
mn35:2.2: He spoke these words before an assembly in Vesali:
mn35:2.3: ‘I see no monk or divine, the head of a sangha, head of a sect, teacher of a sect, even if he claims to be Arahant and Fully Enlightened, who would not shake and shiver and tremble and sweat under the armpits on being engaged in argument with me.
mn35:2.4: Even if I engaged a senseless post in argument it would shake and shiver and tremble on being engaged in argument with me,
mn35:2.5: so what shall I say of a human being?’
mn35:3.1: Then it being morning, the venerable Assaji dressed, and taking his bowl and (outer) robe, he went into Vesali for alms.
mn35:3.2: As Saccaka the Nigantha’s son was walking and wandering for exercise in Vesāli, he saw the venerable Assaji coming in the distance.
mn35:3.3: When he saw him, he went up to him and exchanged greetings with him,
mn35:3.4: and when the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he stood at one side. Then Saccaka the Nigantha’s son said:
mn35:4.1: ‘How does the monk Gotama discipline disciples, Master Assaji; and in what way is the monk Gotama’s instruction usually presented among disciples?’
mn35:4.2: ‘This is how the Blessed One disciplines disciples, Aggivessana; and in this way the Blessed One’s instruction is usually presented among disciples:
mn35:4.3: “Bhikkhus, form is impermanent, feeling is impermanent, perception is impermanent, formations are impermanent, consciousness is impermanent;
mn35:4.4: form is not self, feeling is not self, perception is not self, formations are not self, consciousness is not self;
mn35:4.5: formations are all impermanent, dhammas are all not self.”
mn35:4.6: That is the way the Blessed One disciplines disciples; and that is the way in which the Blessed One’s instruction is usually presented among disciples.’
mn35:4.7: ‘If this is what the monk Gotama asserts, we hear indeed what is ill hearing.
mn35:4.8: Now suppose, sometime or other, we were to meet Master Gotama, suppose we had some conversation with him? Suppose we were to detach him from that evil view?’
mn35:5.1: Now at that time five hundred Licchavis had met together in an assembly hall for some business or other.
mn35:5.2: Then Saccaka the Nigantha’s son went to them and said:
mn35:5.3: ‘Come forth, Licchavis, sirs, come forth. There will be converse today between me and the monk Gotama.
mn35:5.4: If the monk Gotama maintains to me what was maintained to me by one of his famous pupils, the bhikkhu called Assaji, then, just as a strong man might seize a long-haired ram by the hair and drag him to, and drag him fro, and drag him round about;
mn35:5.5: so with argument I will drag the monk Gotama to, and drag him fro, and drag him round about.
mn35:5.6: Just as a strong brewer’s workman might throw a big brewer’s sieve into a deep water tank, and taking it by the corners, drag it to, and drag it fro and drag it round about;
mn35:5.7: so with argument I will drag the monk Gotama to, drag him fro and drag him round about.
mn35:5.8: Just as a strong brewer’s mixer might take a strainer by the corners and shake it down and shake it up and thump it about;
mn35:5.9: so with argument I will shake the monk Gotama down and shake him up and thump him.
mn35:5.10: And just as a sixty year old elephant might go down into a pond and have great sport in the game of hemp-washing,
mn35:5.11: so too I shall have great sport, I fancy, in the game of hemp-washing the monk Gotama.
mn35:5.12: Come forth, Licchavis, sirs, come forth. There will be converse today between me and the monk Gotama.’
mn35:6.2: ‘Now will the monk Gotama refute Saccaka the Nigantha son’s assertions; or will Saccaka the Nigantha’s son refute the monk Gotama’s assertions?’
mn35:6.4: ‘How will Saccaka the Nigantha’s son refute the Blessed One’s assertions; on the contrary, the Blessed One will refute Saccaka the Nigantha son’s assertions.’
mn35:6.5: Then Saccaka the Nigantha’s son went with the five hundred Licchavis to the Hall with the Peaked Roof in the Great Wood.
mn35:7.1: Now on that occasion a number of bhikkhus were walking up and down in the open.
mn35:7.2: Then Saccaka the Nigantha’s son went up to them and asked:
mn35:7.3: ‘Where is Master Gotama living now, sirs.
mn35:7.4: We want to see Master Gotama.’
mn35:7.5: ‘The Blessed One has gone into the Great Wood, Aggivessana, and is sitting at the root of a tree for the day’s abiding.’
mn35:8.1: Then Saccaka the Nigantha’s son went together with a large following of Licchavis into the Great Wood to where the Blessed One was and exchanged greetings with him,
mn35:8.2: and after the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down at one side.
mn35:8.3: And some of the Licchavis paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down at one side; some exchanged greetings with him, and when this courteous and amiable talk was finished, they sat down at one side; some raised their hands palms together in salutation and sat down at one side; some pronounced their name and clan in the Blessed One’s presence and sat down at one side; some kept silence and sat down at one side.
mn35:9.1: When Saccaka the Nigantha’s son had sat down, he said to the Blessed One:
mn35:9.2: ‘I would question Master Gotama on a certain point, if Master Gotama would grant me the favour of an answer to the question?’
mn35:9.4: ‘How does Master Gotama discipline (lead away) his disciples; and in what way is Master Gotama’s instruction usually presented among the disciples?’
mn35:9.5: ‘This is how I discipline (lead away) disciples, Aggivessana; and this is the way my instruction is usually presented among disciples:
mn35:9.6: Form is impermanent, feeling is impermanent, perception is impermanent, formations are impermanent, consciousness is impermanent;
mn35:9.7: form is not self, feeling is not self, perception is not self, formations are not self, consciousness is not self;
mn35:9.8: formations are all impermanent, dhammas are all not self.
mn35:9.9: That is the way I discipline disciples; and that is the way in which my instruction is usually presented among disciples.’
mn35:10.1: ‘A simile occurs to me, Master Gotama.’
mn35:10.2: ‘Let it occur to you, Aggivessana,’ the Blessed One said.
mn35:10.3: ‘Just as when seeds and plants, whatever their kind, reach growth, all do so in dependence on earth, based upon earth;
mn35:10.4: in this way these seeds and plants reach growth, increase and expansion.
mn35:10.5: And just as when the kinds of work to be done by the strong are done, all are done in dependence on earth, based upon earth—
mn35:10.6: in this way these works to be done by the strong are done.
mn35:10.7: so too, Master Gotama, a man has form as self, he produces merit or demerit based on form. He has feeling as self, he produces merit or demerit based on feeling. He has perception as self, he produces merit or demerit based on perception. He has formations as self, he produces merit or demerit based on formations. He has consciousness as self, he produces merit or demerit based on consciousness.’
mn35:11.2: form is my self, feeling is my self, perception is my self, formations are my self, consciousness is my self?’
mn35:11.4: form is my self, feeling is my self, perception is my self, formations are my self, consciousness is my self. And so does this great multitude.’
mn35:11.5: ‘What has this great multitude to do with you, Aggivessana?
mn35:11.6: Please confine yourself to your own assertion alone.’
mn35:11.8: form is my self, feeling is my self, perception is my self, formations are my self, consciousness is my self.’
mn35:12.1: ‘In that case, Aggivessana, I shall ask you a question in return. Answer it as you like.
mn35:12.2: How do you conceive this, Aggivessana,
mn35:12.3: would a head-anointed warrior-noble king have the power in his own realm
mn35:12.4: to execute those who should be executed, to fine those who should be fined, to banish those who should be banished, for example, King Pasenadi of Kosala, or King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha?’
mn35:12.5: ‘Master Gotama, a head-anointed warrior-noble king would have the power in his own realm
mn35:12.6: to execute those who should be executed, to fine those who should be fined, to banish those who should be banished, for example, King Pasenadi of Kosala, or King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha.
mn35:12.7: For even these (oligarchic) communities and societies
mn35:12.8: such as the Vajjians and the Mallians,
mn35:12.9: have the power in their own realm
mn35:12.10: to execute those who should be executed, to fine those who should be fined, to banish those who should be banished,
mn35:12.11: so all the more so an anointed warrior king such as King Pasenadi of Kosala or King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha.
mn35:12.12: He would have it, Master Gotama, and he would be worthy to have it.’
mn35:13.3: “Form is my self”, have you any such power over that form as:
mn35:13.4: “Let my form be thus; let my form be not thus”?’
mn35:13.5: When this was said, Saccaka the Nigantha’s son was silent.
mn35:13.6: A second time the Blessed One said to him:
mn35:13.7: ‘How do you conceive this, Aggivessana, when you say thus:
mn35:13.8: “Form is my self”, have you any such power over that form as:
mn35:13.9: “Let my form be thus; let my form be not thus”?’
mn35:13.10: A second time Saccaka the Nigantha’s son was silent.
mn35:13.11: Then the Blessed One said to him:
mn35:13.12: ‘Aggivessana, answer now. Now is not the time to be silent.
mn35:13.13: If anyone did not answer when asked a question according to Dhamma up to the third time by the Tathāgata his head would split in seven pieces there and then.’
mn35:14.1: Now on that occasion a thunderbolt-wielding spirit with an iron bolt in his head, burning, blazing, glowing, appeared in the air above Saccaka the Nigantha’s son (thinking):
mn35:14.2: ‘If this Saccaka the Nigantha’s son does not answer when asked a question according to Dhamma up to the third time, I shall split his head into seven pieces here and now.’
mn35:14.3: The Blessed One saw the thunderbolt-wielding spirit and so did Saccaka the Nigantha’s son.
mn35:14.4: Then Saccaka the Nigantha’s son was frightened, terrified and his hair stood on end, and seeking to make the Blessed One his shelter, his asylum and refuge, he said:
mn35:14.5: ‘Ask me, Master Gotama; I will answer.’
mn35:15.3: “Form is my self”, have you any such power over that form as:
mn35:15.4: “Let my form be thus; let my form be not thus”?’
mn35:16.3: What you said before does not agree with what you said after, or what you said after with what you said before.
mn35:16.4: How do you conceive this, Aggivessana,
mn35:16.6: “Feeling is my self”, have you any such power over that feeling as:
mn35:16.7: “Let my feeling be thus; let my feeling be not thus”?’
mn35:17.3: What you said before does not agree with what you said after, or what you said after with what you said before.
mn35:17.4: How do you conceive this, Aggivessana,
mn35:17.6: “Perception is my self”, have you any such power over that perception as:
mn35:17.7: “Let my perception be thus; let my perception be not thus”?’
mn35:18.3: What you said before does not agree with what you said after, or what you said after with what you said before.
mn35:18.4: How do you conceive this, Aggivessana,
mn35:18.6: “Formations are my self”, have you any such power over those formations as:
mn35:18.7: “Let my formations be thus; let my formations be not thus”?’
mn35:19.3: What you said before does not agree with what you said after, or what you said after with what you said before.
mn35:19.4: How do you conceive this, Aggivessana,
mn35:19.6: “Consciousness is my self”, have you any such power over that consciousness as:
mn35:19.7: “Let my consciousness be thus; let my consciousness be not thus”?’
mn35:20.3: What you said before does not agree with what you said after, or what you said after with what you said before.
mn35:20.4: How do you conceive this, Aggivessana,
mn35:20.7: ‘Now is what is impermanent unpleasant or pleasant?’
mn35:20.9: ‘Now is what is impermanent, unpleasant and subject to change fit to be regarded as:
mn35:20.10: “This is mine, this is I, this is my self”?’
mn35:20.12: ‘How do you conceive this, Aggivessana, is feeling permanent or impermanent? …
mn35:20.15: How do you conceive this, Aggivessana,
mn35:20.18: ‘Now is what is impermanent unpleasant or pleasant?’
mn35:20.20: ‘Now is what is impermanent, unpleasant and subject to change fit to be regarded as:
mn35:20.21: “This is mine, this is I, this is my self”?’
mn35:21.2: when a man adheres to suffering, resorts to suffering, accepts suffering, always views suffering as: “This is mine, this is I, this is my self”, would he himself ever fully understand suffering or abide with suffering quite exhausted?’
mn35:21.6: that being so, do you not adhere to suffering, do you not resort to suffering, do you not accept suffering, do you not always view suffering as:
mn35:21.7: “This is mine, this is I, this is my self”?’
mn35:22.1: ‘It is as though a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, took a sharp axe and went to the wood;
mn35:22.2: and there he saw a large plantain trunk, straight, young, with no fruit-bud core.
mn35:22.3: Then he cut off the root, he cut off the crown, and having cut off the crown he unrolled the leaf-sheaths;
mn35:22.4: but as he went on unrolling the leaf-sheaths he would never come even to any sapwood, let alone heartwood.
mn35:22.5: So too, Aggivessana, when you are pressed and questioned and cross-questioned by me about your own assertion, you are empty, vacant and in the wrong.
mn35:22.6: But these words of yours were spoken before this assembly:
mn35:22.7: “I see no monk or divine, the head of a sangha, head of a sect, teacher of a sect, even if he claims to be Arahant and Fully Enlightened, who would not shake and shiver and tremble and sweat under the armpits on being engaged in argument with me.
mn35:22.8: Even if I engaged a senseless post in argument it would shake and shiver and tremble on being engaged in argument with me,
mn35:22.9: so what shall I say of a human being?”
mn35:22.10: Now there are drops of sweat on your forehead and they have soaked through your upper robe and fallen to the ground.
mn35:22.11: But there is no sweat on my body now.’
mn35:22.12: And the Blessed One uncovered his golden-coloured body before the assembly.
mn35:22.13: When this was said, Saccaka the Nigantha’s son sat silent, dismayed, with shoulders drooping and head down, glum and with nothing to say.
mn35:23.1: Then Dummukha the son of the Licchavis, seeing Saccaka the Nigantha’s son thus, said to the Blessed One:
mn35:23.2: ‘A simile occurs to me, Master Gotama.’
mn35:23.4: ‘Suppose, venerable sir, not far from a village or town there were a pond
mn35:23.6: And then a party of boys and girls went out from the town or village to the pond, and they went into the water and pulled the crab out of the water and put it on dry land.
mn35:23.7: And whenever the crab extended a leg, they cut it off, broke it, smashed it with sticks and stones,
mn35:23.8: so that the crab with all its legs cut off, broken and smashed would be unable to get back to the pond as before—
mn35:23.9: so too, all Saccaka the Nigantha’s son’s distortions, paradoxes and travesties have been cut off, broken and smashed by the Blessed One,
mn35:23.10: and now he cannot get near the Blessed One as was the purpose of his words.’
mn35:24.1: When this was said, Saccaka the Nigantha’s son told him:
mn35:24.2: ‘Wait, Dummukkha, wait. We are not treating with you, here we are treating with Master Gotama.
mn35:24.3: Let that talk of ours be, Master Gotama, like that of many a monk and divine
mn35:24.4: it was (just) so many words, I fancy.
mn35:24.5: But how does a disciple of the monk Gotama carry out the message, respond to advice, cross beyond uncertainty, lose his doubts, gain intrepidity, and become independent of others in the Teacher’s message?’
mn35:24.6: ‘Here, Aggivessana, any kind of form—whatever, whether past, future or present, in oneself or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—a disciple of mine sees with right understanding all form as it actually is thus: “This is not mine, this not I, this is not my self.”
mn35:24.10: Any kind of consciousness whatever, whether past, future or present, in oneself or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—a disciple of mine sees with right understanding all consciousness as it actually is thus: “This is not mine, this is not I, this not my self.”
mn35:24.11: This is how a disciple of mine carries out the message, responds to advice, crosses beyond uncertainty, loses his doubts, gains intrepidity and becomes independent of others in the Teacher’s message.’
mn35:25.1: ‘Master Gotama, how does a bhikkhu become an Arahant, with the taints exhausted who has lived the life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached the highest goal, destroyed the fetters of being, and who through right final knowledge is liberated?’
mn35:25.2: ‘Here, Aggivessana, any kind of form whatever, whether past, future or present, in oneself or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, a bhikkhu sees with right understanding all form as it actually is thus: “This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self”, and through not clinging he is liberated.
mn35:25.6: Any kind of consciousness whatever, whether past, future or present, in oneself or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, a bhikkhu sees with right understanding all consciousness as it actually is thus: “This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self”, and through not clinging he is liberated.
mn35:25.7: That is how a bhikkhu becomes an Arahant, with taints exhausted, who has lived the life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached the highest goal, destroyed the fetters of being, and through right final knowledge is liberated.
mn35:26.1: ‘When a bhikkhu’s mind is thus liberated, he possesses three unsurpassabilities:
mn35:26.2: unsurpassability in vision, unsurpassability in practice of the way, and unsurpassability in deliverance.
mn35:26.3: When a bhikkhu is thus liberated, he honours, respects, reveres, and venerates only the Tathāgata:
mn35:26.4: The Blessed One is enlightened and teaches the Dhamma by enlightenment. The Blessed One is controlled and he teaches the Dhamma by control. The Blessed One is serene and he teaches the Dhamma by serenity. The Blessed One has crossed over and he teaches the Dhamma by having crossed over. The Blessed One has attained Nibbāna and he teaches the Dhamma by having attained Nibbāna.’
mn35:27.1: When this was said, Saccaka the Nigantha’s son replied:
mn35:27.2: ‘Master Gotama, we were bold and forward in conceiving Master Gotama to be attackable by argument.
mn35:27.3: A man might be such that he could with impunity attack a mad elephant, yet he could not attack Master Gotama with impunity.
mn35:27.4: A man might be such that he could with impunity attack a blazing mass of fire, yet he could not attack Master Gotama with impunity.
mn35:27.5: A man might be such that he could with impunity attack a terrible poisonous serpent, yet he could not attack Master Gotama with impunity.
mn35:27.6: We were bold and forward in conceiving Master Gotama to be attackable by argument.
mn35:27.7: Let the Blessed One, together with the Sangha of Bhikkhus, accept tomorrow’s meal from me.’
mn35:27.8: The Blessed One accepted in silence.
mn35:28.1: Then knowing that the Blessed One had accepted, he addressed the Licchavis:
mn35:28.2: ‘Hear me, Licchavis, the monk Gotama together with the Sangha of Bhikkhus has been invited by me for tomorrow’s meal.
mn35:28.3: You may bring to me whatever you think is proper for him.’
mn35:29.1: Then when the night was ended the Licchavis brought five hundred ceremonial dishes of milk rice as gifts of food.
mn35:29.2: Then Saccaka the Nigantha’s son had good food of various kinds prepared in his own house, and he had the time announced to the Blessed One:
mn35:29.3: ‘It is time, Master Gotama, the meal is ready.’
mn35:30.1: Then, it being morning, the Blessed One dressed, and taking his bowl and (outer) robe, he went with the Sangha of Bhikkhus to Saccaka the Nigantha’s son’s house, and sat down on the seat made ready.
mn35:30.2: Then with his own hands, Saccaka the Nigantha’s son served and satisfied the Sangha of Bhikkhus headed by the Enlightened One with the various kinds of good food.
mn35:30.3: Then when the Blessed One had eaten and no longer had the bowl in his hand, Saccaka the Nigantha’s son took a low seat and sat down at one side.
mn35:30.4: When he had done so, he said to the Blessed One:
mn35:30.5: ‘Master Gotama, whatever the merit and (expected future) greatness due to merit in (this) act-of-giving, may that be for the happiness of the givers.’
mn35:30.6: ‘Aggivessana, such (merit and expected greatness due to merit) as comes of (giving to) one fit for offerings in the way that you are, (you being) not without lust, not without hate, and not without delusion, will be for the givers (who have given to you);
mn35:30.7: but such as comes of (giving to) one fit for offerings in the way that I am, (I being) without lust, without hate and without delusion, will be for you (who have given to me).
